title: Industry on the Defence Investment Plan: welcome direction but urgent delivery gaps
label: 20 October 2026 · One-off session on the Defence Investment Plan
summary: Industry leaders welcomed the Strategic Defence Review’s direction and the Defence Investment Plan’s focus on autonomy, AI and resilience, but said the DIP lacks the 10-year funding detail and firm programmes industry needs to invest, grow capacity and retain firms. SMEs face particular barriers: slow contracting, weak engagement, unclear SME definitions, security-clearance problems and limited help from the Defence Office for Small Business Growth. Witnesses urged clearer multi-year funding paths to 3–3.5% of GDP, faster procurement, stronger skills programmes and better use of international procurement bodies.

speakers.label: Kevin Craven
speakers.name: Kevin Craven
speakers.role: CEO, ADS (defence and aerospace trade body)

speakers.label: Arnab Dutt
speakers.name: Arnab Dutt
speakers.role: Non-Executive Director, Federation of Small Businesses (procurement & social value lead)

glossary.definition: Defence Investment Plan: the government’s published plan for defence spending and priorities.
Strategic Defence Review: the high-level rethink of UK defence priorities that preceded the DIP.
Ministry of Defence: the government department responsible for defence policy and procurement.
Small or medium-sized enterprise: smaller businesses often critical to defence supply chains.
National Armaments Director: the senior MOD official coordinating armaments and procurement.
Defence, Security and Resilience Bank: proposed UK vehicle to finance defence capacity (subject to DFIS decisions).
Multilateral Defence Mechanism: pooled procurement effort with partners like the Netherlands, Poland, Finland.
NATO Support and Procurement Agency: NATO procurement and logistics agency that the UK uses but could use more.
Capital DEL and Resource DEL: government budget categories for investment and day-to-day spending.
UK Sovereign AI Fund: government initiative to back domestic AI capabilities.
A rapid procurement/testbed approach the MOD uses to buy faster and involve SMEs.

glossary.term: Defence Office for Small Business Growth
glossary.definition: MOD office intended to help SMEs navigate defence contracting; currently small and not yet fully operational.

chapters.title: Direction is welcome, but detail is missing
chapters.takeaway: Industry supports the DIP’s shift to autonomy, AI and readiness, but needs a detailed 10-year, funded programme to invest.

turns.speaker: Lincoln Jopp
turns.text: You welcomed the SDR and DIP direction. Can you give concrete examples where the DIP has turned into real orders or behaviour changes?

turns.speaker: Kevin Craven
turns.text: We welcome the pivot to integrated systems, autonomy and AI, and rapid procurement has happened—£1.4bn for defence AI and some rapid tech buys—but the DIP focuses granularity on the first four years and leaves the 10-year picture vague.

turns.speaker: Julian David
turns.text: Tech members expected more orders, especially for SMEs. Our surveys show declines, funding delays hit most firms, and many are reassessing investment or recruitment for defence work.

turns.speaker: Kevin Craven
turns.text: Equipment spend actually fell by £5bn to March 2026 versus the prior year—industry sees rhetoric, but orders are hard to pin down for long-term investing.

turns.speaker: Stephen Phipson
turns.text: There are pockets of change—energetics, cheap one-way effectors, drones—bringing non-traditional suppliers in. But these are small compared with the scale the DIP implies.

turns.speaker: Lincoln Jopp
turns.text: So, strategic intent yes, but not enough medium-term certainty for big industrial investment?

turns.speaker: Kevin Craven
turns.text: Exactly. Intent isn’t the same as an investable, funded plan that lets firms scale production lines and skills over a decade.

chapters.title: SMEs still struggle to access MOD opportunity
chapters.takeaway: SMEs face visibility, contracting, payment and clearance barriers; the SME office exists but is under-resourced.

turns.speaker: Arnab Dutt
turns.text: The DIP is welcome but high-level. Most small firms don't use pipeline documents to find contracts—only 13% do. 62% say finding public opportunities is very difficult.

turns.speaker: Lincoln Jopp
turns.text: Has the MOD’s SME hub helped?

turns.speaker: Arnab Dutt
turns.text: Engagement has been very sparse. Promised regular contact hasn’t materialised; many SMEs that tried working with MOD say they won’t again because of systemic barriers.

turns.speaker: Kevin Craven
turns.text: Some primes have improved—Lockheed Martin, BAE, Babcock are cited for better supplier terms—but progress is patchy and depends on the primes' own certainty.

turns.speaker: Julian David
turns.text: MOD uses a non-standard SME definition and SMEs are being hit by changes in security-clearance sponsorship; firms have lost hundreds of clearances and are reapplying.

turns.speaker: Jesse Norman
turns.text: What do you want from the Defence Office for Small Business Growth?

turns.speaker: Kevin Craven
turns.text: It should be far more than signposting: scale it to the staff numbers proposed, publish best practice (like Commercial X) and actively champion SMEs across MOD procurement.

turns.speaker: Stephen Phipson
turns.text: They are meant to reach full operational capability by year-end. A single front door is a good idea, but it must advocate and measure impact, not just show-and-tell.

chapters.title: Money matters: backloading, efficiency claims and the 3% target
chapters.takeaway: Industry needs a funded multi-year path to 3–3.5% GDP now; backloading and efficiency-dependent funding undermine investment and jobs.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The DIP backloads investment after 2030 and relies on £15bn partly from efficiency savings. Can industry bring spending forward if needed?

turns.speaker: Kevin Craven
turns.text: You can’t switch on production overnight. With advance notice we can build capacity, but new production lines take 2–4 years and need investable certainty now.

turns.speaker: Ian Roome
turns.text: If the next spending review fails to give a funded path to 3% of GDP, will industry still invest?

turns.speaker: Stephen Phipson
turns.text: No. Firms need certainty before they commit to factories and major programmes. The DIP gives themes but not the funded programmes that persuade investors.

turns.speaker: Kevin Craven
turns.text: On jobs: ADS estimates an extra 50,000 jobs at 3% and another 85,000 by 2035 at 3.5%. Those are real economic benefits tied to the funding path.

turns.speaker: Julian David
turns.text: Delays create a learned behaviour of not investing here. Capital goes where there is clarity—US and European markets look more attractive right now.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: So you want a clear path to 3.5% now, not delayed into a future spending review?

turns.speaker: Kevin Craven
turns.text: Yes. A firm, multi-year, funded signal to industry and allies is essential to maintain capacity, exports and allied confidence.

chapters.title: Skills, costs and industrial competitiveness
chapters.takeaway: The UK has engineering talent and manufacturing capacity, but skills gaps, high costs and slow infrastructure block conversion and retention.

turns.speaker: Michelle Scrogham
turns.text: Defence inflation is running above general inflation. Are workforce, supply chain uncertainty and the wider investment environment the drivers?

turns.speaker: Kevin Craven
turns.text: Yes. Plus policy choices like steel tariffs and other business costs hurt competitiveness. Government can help with skills and the business environment.

turns.speaker: Stephen Phipson
turns.text: The big issue is vocational skills and FE capacity. SMEs struggle to find colleges to place apprentices because apprentice funding hasn’t been reformed since 2016.

turns.speaker: Julian David
turns.text: Tech skills are sought after and infrastructure (data centres, connections) is slow and costly here—planning delays mean firms invest elsewhere.

turns.speaker: Michelle Scrogham
turns.text: Could we repurpose automotive factories as Germany has?

turns.speaker: Stephen Phipson
turns.text: Yes—automotive companies want to help, and capacity exists, but they need clear programmes to decide where to invest.

turns.speaker: Michelle Scrogham
turns.text: Have you seen attacks on defence execs affecting the sector?

turns.speaker: Kevin Craven
turns.text: Yes. There’s been an escalation from protesting premises to targeting individuals. That harms morale and could deter people and investors.

chapters.title: Finance, AI and international instruments
chapters.takeaway: Private finance can help, but DFIS must make defence investable; MoD should use NATO procurement more and align AI/tech funds to defence needs.

turns.speaker: Fred Thomas
turns.text: What should the Defence Finance and Investment Strategy clarify to unlock private capital?

turns.speaker: Kevin Craven
turns.text: It must show investable markets, sensible risk-sharing, and SME finance routes for working capital, bonding and insurance; defence infrastructure deals are attractive to private finance.

turns.speaker: Stephen Phipson
turns.text: Series B / growth-stage capital is a UK weakness. Start-up funding exists, but patient domestic capital to scale factories is thin; many deals go to US investors.

turns.speaker: Fred Thomas
turns.text: How current is the DIP on AI and emerging tech? Is Government procurement keeping pace?

turns.speaker: Julian David
turns.text: The DIP needn’t chase every model. But Defence must move to software-first procurement and secure compute/comms so kit can be upgraded. SovAI and other funds exist, but they aren’t obviously tied to defence needs.

turns.speaker: Jesse Norman
turns.text: What about the UK definition of a ‘UK company’—how should sovereignty be judged?

turns.speaker: Julian David
turns.text: Define it by capability, control and choice—what we call 'confident sovereignty'—not merely where a company is registered. That protects supply without blanket protectionism.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Final quick point: why isn't the MOD using the NATO Support and Procurement Agency more?

turns.speaker: Kevin Craven
turns.text: We used to be the 5th largest user of NSPA; now we're 8th while NSPA budgets have tripled. The UK should use it more; it helps scale procurement and access allies’ buying power.

turns.speaker: Stephen Phipson
turns.text: We don't need another procurement agency; better use of existing NATO mechanisms and merging finance vehicles (DSRB/MDM) where sensible would avoid duplication.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you all. In short: the DIP sets a welcome direction, but industry needs funded, granular, multi-year plans, clearer engagement with SMEs, faster procurement, stronger skills and better use of international instruments.
